newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean strikes fizzle as workers retreat.
newsitem.headline: South Korean strikes fizzle as workers retreat.

text.p: White-collar workers joined 40,000 car and shipyard workers in protests on Tuesday but there were few indications the strike had lived up to its billing as the biggest in South Korea's history.
At Pagoda Park in Seoul several thousand bank tellers and securities company workers raised gloved fists in the air and demanded that President Kim Young-sam resign.
Many wore black ties and black silk ribbons in what they said was a symbol of mourning for the death of democracy.

The rally against a controversial new labour law was intended to evoke memories of mass demonstrations in 1987 when white-collar workers joined factory hands and radical students to win a battle for democracy.
But banks stayed open, most manufacturing companies were unscathed and apart from striking taxi drivers public transport ran smoothly. Ports were unaffected.
Military specialists on standby to run trains and telephone services were never needed as union threats to stage the biggest strike in South Korean history fizzled.

The lacklustre response to a call by the Federation of Korean Trade Unions for two days of "all-out" stoppages indicated that the worker militancy that once toppled military-backed rule may be a spent force.
Tuesday's strikes were intended to cap three weeks of wildcat stoppages sparked by the passage of a labour law on December 26 that permitted layoffs, breaking a tradition of jobs-for-life.
Kim's government argues that flexible labour practices will trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness as exports sag.
In by far the biggest protest of the day, about 40,000 workers rallied in a river-side park in the southeast city of Ulsan before marching to the city hall.

No violence was reported but marchers, mostly from the giant Hyundai Group, hurled raw eggs at offices of the ruling New Korea Party and chanted "Down with Kim's government" and "Repeal the labour law".
Office workers along the route threw open their windows and yelled "We're on your side".
Militant workers briefly skirmished with riot police near a Seoul cathederal where union leaders have sought sanctuary from arrest for organising wildcat stoppages.
The officially-sanctioned federation claimed 420,000 of its 1.2 million members were on strike, but the labour ministry put the figure at just more than 50,000.

Nevertheless, the federation and the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions threatened to continue protests until presidential polls in December and said they would combine forces to defeat the New Korea Party candidate unless the law was scrapped.
The confederation vowed its 500,000 members would go ahead with indefinite strikes starting on Wednesday, and some subway and bus drivers indicated they would stop work.

However, the Seoul government has prepared fleets of privately-owned buses to run major routes and subway operators have said non-union drivers will be able to keep services running for several weeks if necessary.
The government has threatened unspecified legal action against international labour leaders visiting Seoul in a gesture of worker solidarity, local media reported.
John Evans, head of a labour advisory body to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said he had been questioned by immigration officials about his activities.
"This is completely normal," he said of his presence as a star attraction at worker rallies. "The abnormality is the attitude of the government."
South Korea formally joined the Paris-based OECD in December, but the new law has upset some of its new partners.
Stock investors took heart from the weak strike response and the leading share index jumped four percent.
